strengths: Principled and rigorous theoretical formulation: The paper applies the Martin-Siggia-Rose-De Dominicis-Janssen (MSRDJ) dynamical mean-field theory to linear / random feature regression with power-law kernel spectra under stochastic Langevin dynamics and L2 regularization.

Unifying framework: The formulation cleanly encompasses several well-known regimes as special cases, including deterministic gradient flow (large beta), Bayesian GP posterior inference (infinite time), and unregularized / regularized settings.

Clear physical insight into learning dynamics and spectral bias: The theory demonstrates how high-dimensional dynamics decouple into independent eigenmodes driven by colored self-consistent noise and retarded by an effective memory kernel (Onsager reaction term), providing an intuitive temporal picture of spectral bias (modes with larger eigenvalues converge exponentially faster).

Analytic characterization of early stopping and scaling laws: Decomposing the test error into bias and variance dynamics allows the authors to derive explicit scaling relations and an optimal stopping time t* ~ (beta/2) * (alpha / (1 + alpha)) balancing bias decay against variance accumulation.

Thorough appendix and consistency checks: The appendix provides extensive derivations, validates that the t -> infinity static limit matches known replica/random matrix results (e.g., Canatar et al., 2021), and explores extensions to label noise.
weaknesses: Heuristic simplification in scaling law derivation: The analytical power laws in Section 5 and Appendix G rely on approximating the memory kernel by a delta function K(t - s) approx delta(t - s) (replacing Q with its expectation). Although motivated as a lower bound, the manuscript does not rigorously establish whether the fluctuation-induced memory kernel alters the asymptotic exponents or only the prefactors.

Inconsistent notation: In Equation (9) the power-law exponent is defined via eta_i = eta_1 i^{-(1+gamma)}, whereas from Appendix B Equation (46) onwards and throughout Section 5, it is denoted as alpha (e.g., eta_k = k^{-(1+alpha)}). Harmonizing the notation throughout the paper would improve readability.

Scope of empirical verification: The numerical validation is conducted exclusively on synthetic Gaussian feature models of moderate dimension (e.g., P = N = 100 or 1000). While this directly verifies the mean-field equations, demonstration on real data or linearized deep networks (e.g., empirical NTK / NNGP regimes) would significantly strengthen the empirical claims.

Claim regarding sample-size independence of optimal stopping time: Equation (36) predicts that t* is entirely independent of sample size P and dimension N, yet Figure 5 only tests t* as a function of beta for fixed P = N = 100. A systematic sweep of t* across multiple values of P would provide much stronger support for this specific claim.

strengths: Principled and rigorous application of the MSRDJ (Martin-Siggia-Rose-De Dominicis-Janssen) path integral formalism to analyze stochastic Langevin gradient dynamics in linear/kernel regression with power-law eigenvalue spectra.

Unifies several regimes into a single dynamical framework, including gradient flow, L2 regularization / weight decay, Bayesian posterior sampling in the stationary limit, and static RKHS spectral bias results (recovering Canatar et al., 2021 as $t \to \infty$).

Provides a clear and intuitive physical picture of early stopping as a dynamical bias-variance trade-off, where large modes are learned rapidly (decaying bias) while noise accumulates over time into the variance term.

Derives an explicit closed-form expression for the compute/time-optimal early stopping point $t^* = \frac{\beta}{2} \frac{\alpha}{1+\alpha}$, showing that under the high-noise approximation, $t^*$ is independent of sample size $P$ and dimension $N$, which is confirmed well by numerical simulations.
weaknesses: A central selling point of the dynamical mean-field theory is the non-local memory kernel $K(t-s)$ that accounts for disorder-induced retardation. However, the explicit scaling laws and the early stopping formula in Section 5 are derived by approximating $K(t-s) \simeq \delta(t-s)$ (the independent Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process approximation). The manuscript does not sufficiently analyze whether and how the memory kernel affects the scaling exponents or prefactors beyond this approximation.

Notation inconsistency between sections: in Eq. (9), the eigenvalue power-law decay exponent is introduced as $\eta_i = \eta_1 i^{-1-\gamma}$, whereas in Eq. (46) and Section 5 the exponent is denoted as $\alpha$ without explicitly stating $\alpha = \gamma$.

Experiments are restricted to synthetic Gaussian features with relatively small system sizes ($N, P \in [100, 1000]$). Demonstrating whether these dynamical scaling regimes and early stopping predictions hold for kernel ridge regression on realistic datasets (e.g., empirical NTK or image datasets with power-law spectra) would significantly strengthen the paper.
The manuscript lacks details on the numerical algorithm used to solve the coupled self-consistent Volterra integral equations (Eqs. 23–30) for the theoretical curves.

strengths: Principled dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) framework: The paper uses the Martin-Siggia-Rose-De Dominicis-Janssen (MSRDJ) path-integral formalism combined with a variational Gaussian approximation to derive self-consistent equations of motion for learning dynamics in feature regression with power-law kernel spectra.

Unifying perspective across training regimes: The formulation naturally accommodates deterministic gradient flow (large beta), stochastic Langevin dynamics (finite beta), and Bayesian posterior sampling (long time limit), rigorously recovering known static replica/cavity results from the literature (e.g., Canatar et al., 2021) as t -> infinity.

Mechanistic understanding of early stopping: The theory cleanly dissects the test error into dynamical bias and variance components, providing an analytical scaling relation for the optimal early stopping time t* as a function of the noise level and spectral decay exponent.

Extensive analytical and numerical verification: The theoretical predictions for the mean mode discrepancy, test error trajectories, and scaling behavior are corroborated by extensive numerical simulations averaged over up to 10^5 realizations.
weaknesses: Simplifying approximation for scaling exponent derivations: While the core DMFT retains full non-Markovian memory through the self-consistent kernel K(t-s), the explicit analytical derivations of the neural scaling exponents and early-stopping time in Section 5 rely on an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck approximation (K(t-s) ~ delta(t-s), effectively replacing Q with its expectation). The paper should more thoroughly discuss the quantitative gap introduced by neglecting memory retardation in these scaling regimes.

Notational and typographic inconsistencies: There are several minor errors in mathematical presentation. In Eq. (9), the eigenvalue power-law exponent is defined with parameter gamma, but from Section 4 onwards (and in Section 5 / Appendix G), the exponent is denoted alpha without explicitly stating the equivalence alpha = gamma. Furthermore, in Eq. (14), the leading minus sign before the summation over Q_ij is omitted, although the subsequent equation (15) restores the correct sign.

Scope restricted to Gaussian linear/kernel features: Although linear regression and kernel models provide standard theoretical testbeds for lazy-learning neural networks, the data model assumes exactly Gaussian features with power-law covariances. The connection to feature learning in non-linear networks remains exploratory (Appendix J).

strengths: The paper formulates a dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) using the Martin-Siggia-Rose-De Dominicis-Janssen (MSRDJ) path-integral formalism combined with a variational Gaussian approximation to describe stochastic Langevin gradient dynamics in random feature/kernel regression with power-law spectra.
The derivation decouples the high-dimensional microscopic weight dynamics into effective single-mode equations driven by a self-consistently determined memory kernel and colored noise.
The theoretical predictions for the mode-wise discrepancy dynamics, test error, and bias-variance decomposition are verified against numerical simulations (for N = P = 100) with good agreement.
weaknesses: Severe discrepancy between claimed contributions and presented results: Despite the title ('Dynamics of neural scaling laws...') and the explicit promise in Section 1 ('obtain analytical results that relate the power-law exponent of the feature kernel, regularization, and early stopping time to obtain a minimal generalization gap'), the manuscript contains neither an analytical derivation of scaling exponents nor a closed-form relation for the optimal early stopping time. Neural scaling laws (e.g., power-law asymptotic decay of test loss with dataset size P or compute/time t) are neither analytically characterized nor empirically plotted.

Limited novelty over existing literature: Dynamical mean-field theory and path-integral approaches to kernel/linear regression have been explored extensively in prior work (e.g., Advani et al., 2020; Bordelon et al., ICML 2024). While the paper argues for a more compact formulation avoiding auxiliary fields, it stops short of Bordelon et al. (2024), who actually derive the power-law scaling exponents across different spectral regimes.

Narrow experimental validation: Simulations are restricted to a single, small system size (N = P = 100) and a single spectral exponent (γ = 0.5). To substantiate claims of asymptotic mean-field behavior and scaling laws, the analysis should validate the theory across varied system sizes, sample sizes P spanning multiple orders of magnitude, and varied spectral exponents γ.

Presentation and writing issues: Several typographic and mathematical notation inconsistencies appear throughout the text (e.g., 'principle components' on page 3; inconsistent bar notation for teacher weights in equations (10)–(12); grammatically awkward phrasing such as 'it effects those weights stronger' on page 6).

strengths: The paper introduces a unified dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) framework based on the Martin-Siggia-Rose-De Dominicis-Janssen (MSRDJ) path-integral formalism to study random feature/linear regression under stochastic Langevin dynamics and L2 regularization.

The theoretical framework naturally produces a dynamic bias-variance decomposition of the test error and explains how time-correlated effective noise drives the growth of variance, formalizing the mechanism behind early stopping.

The analytical predictions for the mode discrepancy evolution, overall test error, and bias-variance decomposition show very good agreement with numerical simulations averaged over $10^5$ realizations.
weaknesses: Mismatch between core claims and actual results: The paper is titled 'Dynamics of neural scaling laws in random feature regression with powerlaw-distributed kernel eigenvalues' and bullet 3 of the contributions claims to 'obtain analytical results that relate the power-law exponent of the feature kernel, regularization, and early stopping time to obtain a minimal generalization gap.' However, no scaling laws (e.g., test loss as a power law of dataset size $P$, parameter count $N$, or training time $t$) are derived or plotted, nor is there any analytical relationship derived connecting the exponent $\gamma$, regularization, and the optimal early stopping time.

Limited empirical/numerical exploration: All numerical experiments are conducted exclusively at a single system size ($P = 100, N = 100$) and a single eigenvalue decay exponent ($\gamma = 0.5$, $\Lambda_{ii} = i^{-1.5}$). There is no sweep over $P$ or $N$ to test the asymptotic mean-field predictions across underparameterized ($P > N$) and overparameterized ($P < N$) regimes, nor across different spectral decay exponents $\gamma$.

Novelty and differentiation relative to prior work: Bordelon, Atanasov, & Pehlevan (ICML 2024; J. Stat. Mech. 2025) previously developed dynamical mean-field theories for learning dynamics with power-law spectra and explicitly analyzed scaling laws. While this submission incorporates finite-temperature Langevin noise and L2 weight decay, it stops short of analyzing the scaling regimes that the title highlights.

Notational and presentation issues: Several mathematical typos exist, such as missing bars denoting teacher weights $ ar{w}_i$ in Eq. (10), (14), and (16), and minor grammatical slips in the text (e.g., 'were modes are pairwise independent' in Appendix C).

strengths: The paper presents a coherent dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) framework based on the MSRDJ path-integral formalism and a variational Gaussian approximation to model the continuous-time dynamics of linear/random feature regression under Langevin noise and L2 regularization.

The theoretical equations of motion decouple into independent eigenmodes coupled only through a scalar memory kernel and an effective self-consistent noise, providing an intuitive mode-by-mode bias-variance decomposition.
Numerical simulations on synthetic data show close quantitative agreement with the integro-differential theoretical predictions for the discrepancy and generalization error curves.
weaknesses: Unsupported central claims regarding neural scaling laws: Despite featuring 'neural scaling laws' in the title and abstract, the manuscript neither derives analytical scaling exponents nor presents empirical evaluations of test error scaling with dataset size P, parameter dimension N, or compute. The paper contains zero scaling plots or power-law scaling analysis.

Missing claimed analytical results on early stopping: The introduction explicitly claims to 'obtain analytical results that relate the power-law exponent of the feature kernel, regularization, and early stopping time to obtain a minimal generalization gap' (page 2, bullet 3). However, no analytical formula or closed-form expression for the optimal early stopping time is provided in either the main text or the appendix.

Incremental conceptual contribution: The qualitative phenomena observed—such as spectral bias (faster learning of top modes), noise accumulation causing test error non-monotonicity, and early stopping acting as regularization—are already well understood in linear regression and kernel models (e.g., Krogh & Hertz 1992; Advani et al. 2020; Canatar et al. 2021; Bordelon et al. 2024). The main addition is combining Langevin noise and L2 regularization in DMFT, but the theoretical depth remains limited.

Extremely restricted experimental scope: All simulations are performed on a single tiny system size (P = N = 100) and a single synthetic power-law exponent (gamma = 0.5). There is no exploration across varying sample sizes P, network dimensions N, spectral decays, or real-data feature kernels.

Notational and presentation errors: Several typos and sloppy descriptions appear in key places. For instance, the caption of Figure 4 incorrectly refers to 'strengths g\beta of the dynamic noise' (where g\beta parameterizes inverse L2 regularization, whereas noise is 2\beta^{-1}); Equation (10) contains a typo '(w_i - w_i)' instead of '(w_i - \bar{w}_i)'; and Equation (26) omits the mode index i on the teacher weight \bar{w}.
